_note: Every figure here is traceable to Aronson & Budhos, Sugar Changed the World (Clarion, 2010), with the page in 'p'. Where the book's own map or text is ambiguous, 'flag' says so rather than inventing precision.

nodes.name: New Guinea
nodes.text: Cane first cultivated by humans — at first simply a wild plant that tasted good.

nodes.name: The Philippines
nodes.text: Cane reaches the Philippines.

nodes.name: India
nodes.text: The first written record of sugar — as an offering burned to reach the gods. Five ingredients: milk, cheese, butter, honey, and sugar cane.

nodes.name: Persia
nodes.text: Darius I invades India; his men find 'a sweet reed that produced honey.'

nodes.name: Mouth of the Indus
nodes.text: Nearchus, sailing for Alexander, finds reeds that 'produce honey, although there are no bees.'

nodes.name: China
nodes.text: First mention of sugar cane in China. Brown sugar was made here for over a thousand years.

nodes.name: Jundi Shapur
nodes.text: The world's first true university. Greeks, Jews, Nestorian Christians and Persians together; the first teaching hospital. By the 600s its doctors wrote about a medicine from India: sharkara.

nodes.name: Arabia
nodes.text: Muhammad begins preaching. By 642 Muslim armies carry the faith — and the knowledge of sugar — across Syria, Iraq, Iran and Egypt.

nodes.name: Egypt
nodes.text: The world's great sugar laboratory. Boil, strain, settle, strain; drain in moulds; mix with milk; boil again. Egypt was known for the 'whitest and purest' sugar.

nodes.name: Al-Andalus
nodes.text: Sugar plantations established across the Muslim Mediterranean and Spain.

nodes.name: Sicily
nodes.text: Later held by Christians, who applied what they had learned from Muslims: how to plant cane and refine sugar.

nodes.name: Cyprus
nodes.text: A fertile Christian-held island where the Muslim plantation model was rebuilt.

nodes.name: The Holy Land
nodes.text: Crusaders find 'certain ripe plants which the common folk called honey cane… In our hunger we chewed them all day.'

nodes.name: The Champagne fairs
nodes.text: Six fairs a year, the one place Europeans could buy the world's goods. Next to the fruits and spices: piles of a medicine called sugar.

nodes.name: Venice
nodes.text: Venice comes to dominate European trade with the Muslim world and greatly expands the sugar trade.

nodes.name: Hawaii
nodes.text: Polynesian seafarers carry cane island to island across the Pacific — the other half of the plant's journey.

nodes.name: Madeira
nodes.text: Portuguese conquest. By 1450 Madeira is a leading sugar producer for Europe.

nodes.name: The Canary Islands
nodes.text: Muslim-style plantations built on the Atlantic islands, some staffed by slaves purchased from nearby Africa. Columbus carried cane from Gomera.

nodes.name: The Azores
nodes.text: Europeans reach the uninhabited Azores.

nodes.name: Hispaniola
nodes.text: On his second voyage, Columbus carries sugar cane plants from Gomera across the Atlantic. Everything after this follows.

arcs.label: the Muslims 'swept past Jundi Shapur and learned the secrets of sugar'
Egyptians at Kublai Khan's court teach white sugar

plantations.name: Madeira
plantations.note: A leading producer for Europe by 1450.

plantations.name: Canary Islands
plantations.note: Columbus took cane from Gomera in 1493.

plantations.name: Hispaniola
plantations.note: Sugar boomed here first — until news of Aztec gold pulled the Spaniards to Mexico.

plantations.name: Brazil (Pernambuco)
plantations.note: Some three million Africans taken to Brazil over four hundred years. 'Without sugar, no Brazil; without slaves, no sugar; without Angola, no slaves.'

plantations.name: Barbados
plantations.note: 166 square miles. 252,500 enslaved Africans brought between 1701 and 1810.

plantations.name: Antigua
plantations.note: Where William Clark painted the ten views used throughout this map.

plantations.name: Montserrat
plantations.note: Equiano: the island 'requires 20,000 new Negroes annually, to fill up the vacant places of the dead.'

plantations.name: Jamaica
plantations.note: 662,400 enslaved Africans brought between 1701 and 1810. In 1750: about 17,000 white people, 7,000 free black and mixed, and some 170,000 enslaved.
plantations.flag: The book dates the English conquest to 1665; the invasion was in fact 1655, with Spain ceding the island in 1670. Worth checking against another source.

plantations.name: Saint-Domingue
plantations.note: By the late 1700s the world centre of sugar. So many plantations that enslaved 'commanders' managed other enslaved people.

plantations.name: Demerara
plantations.note: Where the Whitby and the Hesperus landed the first indentured Indians in 1838.

plantations.name: Cuba
plantations.note: Large-scale planting began in the 1800s with owners interested in modern technology; some led the way in freeing Cuban slaves. Booming Cuban production helped drive cane prices down.

plantations.name: Louisiana
plantations.note: The only American slave state where the native-born enslaved population kept dropping. Planters bought healthy young men in their late teens, expecting them to die by their thirties.

plantations.name: Hawaii
plantations.note: First plantation 1835. Chinese workers from 1852, Japanese from 1868, then Filipinos, Koreans and Portuguese.

slaveTrade.note: The book's map gives three totals and names four destination regions. It does not break the totals down by region, and neither does this map. The named places below carry only figures the book states.

embarkation.name: Angola / West Central Africa
embarkation.text: 'Without Angola, no slaves.' The current that carried Cabral to Brazil by accident in 1500 made this the easiest crossing of all.

embarkation.name: Bight of Benin
embarkation.text: Africans who sold other Africans insisted on being paid in fabrics from India — about 35 percent of the cargo carried from Europe to Africa began in India.

embarkation.name: Gold Coast
embarkation.text: By 1753 British ships were taking an average of 34,250 people from Africa every year. By 1768, 53,100.

embarkation.name: Senegambia
embarkation.text: Many of the soldiers who defeated Britain and France in Haiti were recently arrived Africans — warriors trained in military tactics at home.

destinations.name: Spanish America
destinations.figure: named on the book's map; no total given

destinations.name: French Caribbean
destinations.figure: named on the book's map; no total given

destinations.name: British Caribbean
destinations.figure: named on the book's map; no total given

destinations.name: North America
destinations.figure: about 500,000 — only 4 percent of all Africans taken

keyFacts: Only 4 percent of the people taken from Africa were brought to North America. 96 percent went to the Caribbean, Brazil and the rest of South America — mostly to work with sugar.
Some 500,000 enslaved people were brought to North America, and there were four million African Americans at emancipation.
On the sugar islands more than two million people were brought from Africa, and there were 670,000 at emancipation.
Sugar, with its demand for relentless labour, was a killer.

sphericalTrade.note: The book's argument on p. 37: what textbooks call the Triangle Trade 'was really as round as the globe.'

flows.cargo: fabrics, clothes, manufactured goods — about 35% of it originally from India
flows.because: About a third of what left Europe to buy people in Africa was Indian cloth. Without it London has too little of what buyers on the coast will take.
People were bought, not taken for nothing. Either European trade goods or New England rum has to arrive first — either one will do.
The same condition on the other African coast: something has to arrive to trade with.
The sugar is made by the people who were landed here. No arrivals, no crop.
The same condition, on the other island.

flows.cargo: flour, bread, corn, salted beef, timber
flows.because: Grown and cut on North American farms and forests. Nothing on this map has to arrive first.

flows.cargo: sugar, rum, molasses, limes, cocoa, ginger
flows.because: Also made by the people landed at Barbados — the molasses in this hold is what New England distils.

flows.cargo: rum, traded directly for people — cutting Europe out entirely
flows.because: Newport's rum is distilled from Caribbean molasses. Cutting Europe out does not cut out the islands.

flows.cargo: silver from the mines of Bolivia
flows.because: Dug out of the mountain. Nothing on this map has to arrive first.
Manila is a transfer point. What it sends on is the silver that reached it.

flows.cargo: Indian cloth — the thing that buys the people who make the sugar
flows.because: The cloth is bought with silver. No silver, no cloth going west.

sphericalTrade.systemNote: Explore answers what the parts are and what moves between them. It cannot answer what else stops if one part stops, because a line from A to B does not know what had to reach A first. That is what 'requires' is for. Each flow lists what must arrive before it can run: every group must be satisfied, and within a group any one member will do.
sphericalTrade.systemAssumption: Two readings are built in and worth arguing with. The book draws one European goods flow to Africa, so it stands here for that trade as a whole and both African embarkation flows depend on it. And a flow only counts as running if it can be traced back to something intact — so a loop that holds only itself up (Barbados molasses to Newport, Newport rum to Ouidah, Ouidah people to Barbados) is not enough on its own.

outcome.label: Cheap sugar in an ordinary English teacup
outcome.because: Sugar has to reach Britain from somewhere. Either island will do — which is why knocking out one of them is not enough.
outcome.live: Sugar is cheap enough that an ordinary household sweetens its tea without thinking about it.
outcome.dead: No cheap sugar. The tea is still tea; the sugar is back to being a luxury for people who can afford a luxury.

indenture.note: The book's map: Indian Indentured Workers, 1835–1917 (p. 107). Contracts ran five years at about 24 cents a day, with 8 cents a week deducted for food. The voyage could take 27 weeks — far longer than the Middle Passage.
indenture.passageNote: The sailing track from Calcutta to the Caribbean, outside the book. The book's map draws indenture as straight lines between two points, which sends the Atlantic voyages overland across peninsular India and the Congo. Ships went the only way there was before the Suez Canal: down the Hooghly, across the Bay of Bengal, south over the equator into the Indian Ocean, round the Cape of Good Hope on the Agulhas Current, then northwest across the South Atlantic on the southeast trades. About 10,000 nautical miles; the Whitby took 112 days.
indenture.passageFlag: Waypoints reconstruct the standard course, not the log of any one ship. The named calls are the two the 1838 record actually names.

passage.name: Calcutta
passage.note: The Whitby sailed 13 January 1838 with 249 aboard; the Hesperus followed on 29 January with 165. Both went down the Hooghly, whose silt and shifting bars were the first hazard of the voyage.
Into the Bay of Bengal on the tail of the northeast monsoon.
South across the equator and out into the open Indian Ocean.

passage.name: The Cape of Good Hope
passage.note: Rounded on the warm Agulhas Current, through the gales and swells of the Roaring Forties. The only way from the Indian Ocean to the Atlantic before the Suez Canal.

passage.name: St Helena
passage.note: Passed, not called at. Cholera broke out aboard the Hesperus after the Cape, and the surgeon Theophilus Richmond — 22 years old, his medical stores gone — asked the captain to put in here for chalk powder and laudanum. The captain refused, citing anchorage fees and delay, and said he would stop only if Richmond insisted in law and took on the cost himself. Richmond withdrew the request. Eleven of the ship's thirteen deaths were cholera. The Whitby bypassed island stops altogether.

passage.name: Ascension Island
passage.note: The Hesperus did put in here — for water and ordinary stores, not the medicines that had been refused at St Helena. A remote, arid volcanic island; the only land the ship touched between India and the Caribbean.
Northwest across the South Atlantic on the southeast trade winds.

passage.name: Demerara
passage.note: Both ships reached Demerara on 5 May 1838, the Hesperus late that night. The Whitby then ran east to Berbice to land 164 for Highbury and Waterloo, and came back between 14 and 16 May to put the remaining 80 ashore for Belle Vue.

origins.name: Calcutta
origins.text: The embarkation depot — buildings behind a high wall near the harbour. Recruits were vaccinated, given metal feeding bowls and warm clothes, and a 'tin ticket' worn round the neck.

origins.name: The northern countryside
origins.text: Where the arkatis — the recruiters — went looking. 'You want to make a better wage? There's good work upriver.'

destinations.name: British Guiana (Demerara)
destinations.text: The Whitby, carrying 249 passengers, and the Hesperus, carrying 244, sailed for Demerara in 1838. Marina Budhos's great-grandparents came here.
destinations.flag: The book gives the Hesperus 244. The Calcutta embarkation logs record 165. 244 is the number that came off the Whitby — 249 embarked, less 5 dead at sea — and the two figures appear to have been crossed at some point in the retelling. 414 people embarked on the two ships and 396 landed.

destinations.name: Trinidad
destinations.text: 'E no tell e I go chinedad you know' — Bharath, who was not told where he was going, or that he would never see his parents again.

destinations.name: Mauritius
destinations.text: One of the three colonies the book names alongside British Guiana and Trinidad.

destinations.name: Natal, South Africa
destinations.text: Indians were first brought here to cut cane in 1852. Gandhi arrived in 1894 because they were already here.

destinations.name: Surinam
destinations.text: On the book's map of indenture destinations.

destinations.name: Jamaica
destinations.text: On the book's map of indenture destinations.

destinations.name: Fiji
destinations.text: A major indenture destination in this period. Not named in this book — included so the pattern is complete.

keyFacts: Crossing the 'black water' — the kali pani — meant losing caste. You could not return and be respected without a special ceremony.
On the ships the emigrants called themselves jahajii-bhai — ship brothers.
By the end of the 1800s only about a quarter of the indentured sailed back to India.
Gandhi: indenture was 'almost as bad as slavery. Like the slave the indentured labourer was the property of his master.'

freedom.name: Paris — the Pauline case
freedom.text: Pierre Lemerre the Younger argues for an enslaved woman who wanted to stay in a convent: 'All men are equal.' Sixty years before the Declaration of Independence.

freedom.name: Narragansett Bay — the Polly
freedom.text: 7 April 1765: Rhode Island men, faces blackened, strip a ship of barrel after barrel of molasses rather than pay the sugar tax. Eight years before the Boston Tea Party, and the same issue.

freedom.name: Boston — the General Assembly
freedom.text: 'If Taxes are laid upon us … without ever having a Legal Representative where they are laid, are we not reduced from the Character of Free Subjects to the miserable status of Tributary Slaves?'

freedom.name: Cambridge — a school assignment
freedom.text: 'Is it lawful to make slaves of others against their will?' Thomas Clarkson wrote the winning Latin essay and convinced himself. 'In the day-time I was uneasy. In the night I had little rest.'

freedom.name: Bristol
freedom.text: Even in a port city whose harbour was full of slave ships, newspapers reported 'the popular sentiment has been very strongly expressed against the continuance of that traffick in human flesh.'

freedom.name: Birmingham — the Female Society
freedom.text: Women sewed bags carrying abolitionist images, and read Elizabeth Heyrick's argument that all enslaved people must be freed at once, not gradually.

freedom.name: Peckham — the Ladies Anti-Slavery Association
freedom.text: A pamphlet urging readers to buy only sugar from India, labelled 'Produced by the labour of FREEMEN.' Some 400,000 English people stopped buying slave-grown sugar.

freedom.name: Westminster
freedom.text: At precisely noon on 25 March 1807, George III signed the law banning British involvement in the slave trade. No enslaved person was freed by it. In 1833 the Emancipation Bill followed; on 1 August 1838 slavery ended in the British empire.

freedom.name: Paris — the Bastille
freedom.text: July 1789. In August the National Assembly declares that 'men are born and remain free and equal in rights' — and, in the same document, that 'property is an inviolable and sacred right.' So what were slaves?

freedom.name: Alligator Woods, Saint-Domingue
freedom.text: 14 August 1791: commanders from the richest sugar plantations swear an oath to 'listen to the voice of liberty which speaks in the hearts of all of us' — and to destroy everything related to sugar. Within two months, some one thousand plantations were demolished.

freedom.name: Palmares
freedom.text: For nearly a century, a nation of escaped African, Native American and even white slaves in the mountains behind Brazil's coastal plantations. At its peak 20,000 to 30,000 people. Zumbi is honoured in Brazil today as a great ancestor.

freedom.name: Cockpit Country, Jamaica
freedom.text: Maroons the British could not defeat. A peace treaty in 1739–40; sixty years later, with Haiti in revolt, Britain broke its word and deported as many as it could to Canada. Their descendants still live in Jamaica.

freedom.name: Demerara — the 1823 rising
freedom.text: Over three thousand enslaved people rose after hearing John Smith preach Moses leading the Jews out of Egypt. Asked what they wanted, they answered: 'Our rights.' Quamina was hanged in chains at the entrance to Gladstone's plantation; Smith was sentenced to death and died before his ship reached London.

freedom.name: The German Coast, Louisiana
freedom.text: Charles Deslondes, a free man of colour from Saint-Domingue, led what is sometimes called the largest slave revolt in US history. Sixty-six enslaved people were killed, and two whites. The rebellion failed — and marked the link between Louisiana and Haiti.

freedom.name: Cap-Français
freedom.text: 1 January 1804: the Republic of Haiti is born. The former slaves had defeated first England, then France. Jefferson refused to recognise it; the United States did not do so until 1862.

freedom.name: Durban, Natal
freedom.text: Gandhi arrives to practise law because Indians were already here, cutting cane. A man came to him 'in tattered clothes, headgear in hand, two front teeth broken and his mouth bleeding' — Balasumdaram, beaten by his employer and unable to leave.

freedom.name: Empire Theatre, Johannesburg
freedom.text: 11 September 1906. Gandhi invites everyone present to swear not to register under the Black Act — each person facing 'not to his neighbor, but his God.' Every hand went up.

freedom.name: Hamidia Mosque, Johannesburg
freedom.text: 16 August 1908: the certificates of 2,300 Indians burned in a great iron cauldron — the first major act of Satyagraha. By June 1914 the Black Act was off the books.

freedom.name: Delhi
freedom.text: India becomes the first British colony since the United States to break free from foreign rule. Satyagraha would go on to shape Martin Luther King Jr. and the American civil rights movement.

science.name: Berlin — Andreas Marggraf
science.text: He dried and mashed parsnips, then beets, and extracted what made them sweet. It was identical to the sugar from cane. For the first time a taste native to the tropics was matched by a plant grown in a cold place.

science.name: France — 334 beet factories
science.text: Napoleon, locked out of the Caribbean by the British navy and by the Haitians, ordered thousands of acres of beets planted. By 1814 France had more than three hundred factories turning beets into sugar.

science.name: New Orleans — Norbert Rillieux
science.text: Born in 1806 to a wealthy white planter and a free woman of colour, educated in France, he worked out that heating syrup in a series of sealed pans instead of open cauldrons transformed the whole process. One person could do what a team had done. He returned to France because being a noted inventor was no guarantee of safety for a Black man in Louisiana.

science.name: The northern Ukraine
science.text: The one part of the Russian empire where landowners were trying new tools and new ideas. When word of beet sugar arrived they knew what to do. Marc Aronson's family story begins here — with a serf who found a way to give raw beet sugar sparkling hues, and made enough money to buy his freedom.

science.name: Russia — the serfs are freed
science.text: Two years before the Emancipation Proclamation. Beet sugar had set an example of modern farming that helped convince Russian nobles it was time.

science.name: Sugar City, Colorado
science.text: Harvesting beets was not as deadly as cutting cane, but it was hard work for little pay. Lewis Hine photographed children aged ten to eighteen working these fields.

science.name: Brazil — cane into fuel
science.text: The land that imported more Africans than any other still has perfect soil for cane. Today much of the crop becomes ethanol.

consumption.note: Sugar eaten per person per year, in pounds (p. 65–69, 116).

england.label: 1800 — England, a 450% rise in one century

comparisons.label: United States today, cane sugar only

production.label: 1800 — world production, almost all sent to Europe
